title: Structural Hazards
summary: What happens when two in-flight instructions both need the same piece of hardware at once, and the two ways designers resolve it.

slides.markdown:
A **structural hazard** is the simplest kind of pipeline conflict: two instructions, at the same moment, both need the exact same piece of physical hardware.

Think of two chefs needing the one shared oven at the same instant — someone has to wait, or the kitchen needs a second oven. Pipelines resolve structural hazards the same two ways: **duplicate the resource**, or **make one instruction stall**.

slides.subTitle: What counts as a structural hazard
slides.markdown:
A structural hazard occurs purely because of **hardware scarcity**, not because one instruction's data depends on another's. Two instructions could be entirely unrelated computationally and still collide if they both need, say, the single write port on the register file in the same cycle.

This is the easiest hazard type to reason about: no dependency analysis needed, just "do these two stages, active this cycle, both reach for the same physical unit?"

slides.subTitle: One memory, two consumers
slides.markdown:
The textbook example: a single memory port must serve both **instruction fetch** (every cycle, for every instruction) and **data access** (whenever a load or store reaches MEM). If instruction 4 is fetching in the same cycle that instruction 1 is doing a data load, both want the memory port simultaneously.

In a 5-stage pipeline this collision is common — fetch happens every cycle, and roughly one in every few instructions is a load or store — so this exact hazard motivated one of the most standard fixes in real CPU design.

slides.subTitle: Duplicate the resource
slides.markdown:
The most common real fix: give fetch and data access **separate hardware** entirely — a split instruction cache (I-cache) and data cache (D-cache), each with its own port into memory. Now IF and MEM can both run every cycle without ever contending.

This is why almost every real CPU has split L1 instruction and data caches rather than one unified L1 — it isn't primarily about capacity, it's about eliminating this exact structural hazard on the most heavily used resource in the pipeline.

slides.subTitle: Stall instead
slides.markdown:
When duplicating hardware is too expensive or the conflict is rare, the alternative is to **stall** — insert a bubble that holds one instruction (typically the younger one) in place for a cycle while the other uses the shared resource. The stalled instruction's stage does no useful work that cycle, and everything behind it in the pipeline waits too.

Stalling costs a real cycle of throughput every time the hazard occurs, but avoids the area and power cost of a second copy of hardware that would otherwise sit idle most of the time.

slides.subTitle: A bubble in the pipeline
slides.markdown:
A single-port-memory design forces instruction 4's fetch to wait one cycle because instruction 1 is using the shared port for its data access that cycle.

![A pipeline bubble stalling one instruction's fetch stage to free a shared memory port](assets/structural-hazard-stall-bubble.svg)

The bubble ripples forward: every instruction behind the stalled one is delayed a cycle too, since none can occupy a stage it still holds.

assets.alt: A pipeline bubble stalling one instruction's fetch stage to free a shared memory port

slides.subTitle: Duplication vs stalling
slides.markdown:
| | Duplicate hardware | Stall |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput cost | None once built | One bubble per conflict |
| Area / power cost | Extra unit, always present | None extra |
| Best when | Conflict is frequent (e.g. every-cycle fetch) | Conflict is rare or duplication is too costly |

The decision comes down to how often the hazard actually fires. Split I-caches and D-caches are worth the extra silicon because fetch contends with data access constantly; a rarely-used specialized functional unit might be cheaper to just occasionally stall for.

slides.sectionTitle: A different flavor: a busy functional unit
slides.subTitle: Non-pipelined dividers cause the same conflict
slides.markdown:
Register-file ports and memory ports aren't the only source of structural hazards. A **multi-cycle, non-pipelined divider** is a common one: division typically takes far more cycles than an add or multiply, and if the divider itself isn't pipelined internally, a second divide instruction simply cannot enter it until the first one finishes.

The fix pattern is the same menu as before — either build multiple divider units (expensive; division is already the most area-hungry ALU operation) or stall the second divide until the first drains. Most real designs choose to stall here, on the reasoning that back-to-back divides are rare in typical code, unlike the every-cycle fetch/data-access conflict that justifies paying for a split cache.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: turning a hazard rate into CPI
slides.subTitle: How often a stall actually shows up
slides.markdown:
Suppose 2% of instruction pairs hit a structural hazard (say, a rare shared-port conflict), each costing a 1-cycle stall, on top of a base CPI of 1.0:

```
stall contribution = 0.02 * 1 cycle = 0.02
effective CPI = 1.0 + 0.02 = 1.02
```

A 2% conflict rate barely moves CPI — this is exactly why designers tolerate rare structural hazards with a stall instead of paying for duplicate hardware. Compare this to the unified memory-port case from earlier: if fetch and data access collide on *every* load/store instruction (say 30% of instructions are loads/stores, all colliding), the same 1-cycle stall costs `0.30 * 1 = 0.30` — fifteen times worse. The frequency of the conflict, not just its per-occurrence cost, is what decides whether duplicating hardware is worth it.
